title: Invent a chess variant: change exactly one rule
description: Keep the board, keep the pieces, change ONE rule — and you have invented a chess variant. The discipline of changing only one thing is what makes the experiment fair, fun and endlessly repeatable.

body.heading: Pick your one rule
paragraphs: Choose a single change and write it down before you play: pawns may move two squares every move, the queen moves like a knight as well, or a captured piece returns to its owner's side of the board. One change only — two changes and you no longer know which one made the game sing or collapse.
Agree the exact wording together and settle disputes by the written rule, not by volume. Real variant inventors — and there are thousands of published chess variants — live by that written line.

body.heading: Play, judge, record
paragraphs: Play at least two games with the variant before judging it; the first game is mostly surprise. Then record the verdict in a notebook: what the rule changed, whether games got shorter or wilder, and your star rating.
Next week, change a different rule — or hand your variant to another pair of players and watch them find the loopholes you missed. A variant that survives strangers is a real invention.

takeaway: Change exactly one written rule, play it twice before judging, and record the verdict: that is how a chess variant is invented, tested and improved.
materials: A notebook and pencil for the written rule and verdicts
supervision: An adult should join or supervise games with younger players and keep captured pieces counted and off the floor.
safetyNotes: Keep small chess pieces away from children under three and from pets.
Play seated at a table so pieces are not lost underfoot.
Agree the written rule before the first move to keep arguments friendly.
